questions.question: Uniform beam equilibrium with a clockwise couple
questions.subtopic: Moments, kinematics graphs, material strains and Young modulus
questions.prompt: A uniform horizontal beam of length 4.00 m and mass 12.0 kg is supported at a pivot 1.50 m from its left end. A vertical downward force of 50.0 N acts at the left end. Another unknown downward force P acts at the right end. An additional clockwise couple has moment 8.00 N m. The beam is in equilibrium. Take g=9.80 N kg⁻¹. Find P and the vertical reaction at the pivot. Explain why the couple adds a moment but no resultant force. [9 marks]
markPoints: Places the uniform beam's weight at its centre x=2.00 m.
Calculates beam weight W=12.0×9.80=117.6 N.
Takes moments about the pivot and identifies 50.0×1.50=75.0 N m anticlockwise.
Identifies beam's clockwise moment 117.6×0.50=58.8 N m.
Accounts for the extra clockwise pure-couple moment of 8.00 N m.
Writes moment equilibrium 75.0=58.8+8.00+2.50P.
Solves P=3.28 N downwards.
Uses vertical equilibrium to find upward pivot reaction 50.0+117.6+3.28=170.88 N, ≈171 N.
Explains a pure couple is two equal and opposite separated forces: net force zero but non-zero turning moment, independent of pivot location.
questions.modelAnswer: For a uniform beam, the weight W=12.0×9.80=117.6 N acts at the midpoint, x=2.00 m. Moments about the pivot x=1.50 m: the left load produces 50.0×1.50=75.0 N m anticlockwise. The beam weight gives 117.6×(2.00−1.50)=58.8 N m clockwise; the applied couple adds 8.00 N m clockwise; and the right load P gives 2.50P clockwise. Therefore 75.0=58.8+8.00+2.50P, giving P=3.28 N. Vertical equilibrium gives pivot reaction R=50.0+117.6+3.28=170.88≈171 N upwards. A couple creates torque but no net force, so it changes moments but not the vertical force equation.

questions.question: Signed displacement and total distance from changing velocity
questions.subtopic: Moments, kinematics graphs, material strains and Young modulus
questions.prompt: A body moves along a straight line. Its velocity increases uniformly from 0 m s⁻¹ at t=0 to +6.0 m s⁻¹ at t=3.0 s, then decreases uniformly to −2.0 m s⁻¹ at t=5.0 s. Sketch the velocity-time graph, calculate acceleration in each interval, state when the direction changes, and find both net displacement and total distance by 5.0 s. [8 marks]
markPoints: Draws a continuous piecewise-linear velocity-time graph through (0,0), (3,6), (5,−2).
Finds acceleration 0–3 s as +2.0 m s⁻².
Finds acceleration 3–5 s as −4.0 m s⁻².
Finds v=0 at t=4.5 s, where the direction reverses.
Calculates signed area 0–3 s as +9.0 m.
Calculates signed area 3–5 s as +4.0 m, including the negative part.
Finds net displacement +13.0 m.
Uses absolute areas (9.0+4.5+0.5) to find total distance 14.0 m.
questions.modelAnswer: The graph joins (0,0), (3,6) and (5,−2) with straight segments. Acceleration in the first part is 6/3=+2.0 m s⁻²; next it is (−2−6)/(5−3)=−4.0 m s⁻². After 1.5 s of the second segment, velocity falls to zero, so reversal occurs at t=4.5 s. Signed area 0–3: ½×3×6=9 m. Signed area 3–5: ((6+−2)/2)×2=4 m, consisting of +4.5 m and −0.5 m. Net displacement=9+4=+13 m. Total distance=9+4.5+0.5=14 m. The drawn graph must be manually checked.

questions.question: Sketch elastic, plastic and fracture regions of a ductile stress-strain curve
questions.subtopic: Moments, kinematics graphs, material strains and Young modulus
questions.prompt: Sketch a qualitative tensile stress–strain curve for a ductile material. Label the initial proportional region, limit of proportionality, a later elastic limit, plastic deformation and fracture. On the same axes show a possible straight unloading line from a point beyond the elastic limit before fracture, indicating permanent strain. Explain why losing proportionality does not automatically mean permanent deformation. [7 marks]
markPoints: Draws tensile stress on the vertical axis and tensile strain on the horizontal axis.
Shows an initial straight-line elastic region through the origin.
Labels the limit of proportionality where the relation becomes nonlinear.
Indicates a distinguishable elastic limit beyond which unloading leaves permanent strain.
Shows a further plastic-deformation region continuing towards fracture.
Shows an unloading line from within the plastic region meeting the strain axis at positive non-zero strain.
Explains nonlinear deformation can remain reversible before the elastic limit, while unloading from the plastic region leaves permanent strain.
questions.modelAnswer: Sketch a stress-versus-strain curve beginning as a line from the origin (Hooke's-law proportional region). Mark where it first departs from straight-line behaviour as the limit of proportionality, with the elastic limit later or at that point depending on the schematic material. Beyond the elastic limit show a plastic region and eventually fracture. From a plastic-region point draw an approximately straight unloading path back to the strain axis at positive strain, showing permanent deformation. A departure from proportionality does not by itself prove permanent strain: some nonlinear extension may be reversible. Judge drawing marks manually.

questions.question: Young modulus and diameter-based uncertainty
questions.subtopic: Moments, kinematics graphs, material strains and Young modulus
questions.prompt: An idealised wire has original length L=1.50 m, diameter d=(0.300±0.010) mm and extends by ΔL=(1.20±0.02) mm under force F=12.0 N. Assume uncertainty in force and length is negligible. Calculate the original cross-sectional area, Young modulus and approximate percentage uncertainty in Young modulus using the addition-of-percentage-uncertainties rule. [8 marks]
markPoints: Converts d=0.300 mm to 3.00×10⁻⁴ m.
Uses A=πd²/4 for the circular area.
Calculates A≈7.07×10⁻⁸ m².
Converts extension 1.20 mm to 1.20×10⁻³ m.
Uses E=FL/(AΔL) with consistent SI quantities.
Calculates E≈2.12×10¹¹ Pa.
Calculates diameter contribution to area uncertainty 2×(0.010/0.300)×100≈6.67%.
Calculates extension contribution (0.02/1.20)×100≈1.67%, giving total relative E uncertainty≈8.33% with stated assumption.
questions.modelAnswer: d=0.300×10⁻³=3.00×10⁻⁴ m. A=πd²/4=π(3.00×10⁻⁴)²/4≈7.0686×10⁻⁸ m². ΔL=1.20×10⁻³ m. E=FL/(AΔL)=(12.0×1.50)/(7.0686×10⁻⁸×1.20×10⁻³)≈2.12×10¹¹ Pa. Since A∝d², percentage area uncertainty≈2×(0.010/0.300)×100=6.67%; extension uncertainty≈(0.02/1.20)×100=1.67%. With force and length uncertainties negligible, approximate percentage uncertainty in E≈6.67+1.67=8.33%.
